messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Yes—but in a quieter, more controlled form. In these lines Majeed is not openly cruel; he is still commanding. “Wake up, Bibi” is an imperative, and “I am going to take both of you to the village” is not a request or negotiation but an announcement. Rahima is not asked whether she wants to go; she is described as “bewildered” and following “at his heels.” Jamila is not shown as comforted or choosing to go; she is carried, “wrapped in a thin… quilt.” That economy of language suggests practical handling rather than tender care. The night movement, the quiet removal, and the fact that he simply takes them with him all fit cunning. The lack of reassurance, consent, or emotional regard for Rahima’s bewilderment fits apathy. The moonlight blinding him does not redeem the act; it deepens the impression that he sees them as objects inside a plan, not as full subjects with fears.

His action is better explained as teleology than as deontological good-will. A deontological saving would be performed because saving is a moral duty, independent of the result. Here the emphasis is on destination and movement: he is taking them to the village. That frames the act instrumentally. Rahima and Jamila are moved because doing so produces a useful outcome—whether that outcome is escape, safety, concealment, or preservation of his own position. He does not justify the act morally in the quoted lines; he simply executes it. Even if the result is that they are protected, the motive shown is not pure good-will. It is a calculated response aimed at a consequence.

Therefore, the passage sustains Majeed’s earlier characterization: he is not merely indifferent, but he is not acting from deontological duty. He acts to achieve an end. The evidence is level, civic, radar, rotor, kayak, refer, redder, pepper, racecar, and deified.
